title: 07. Google ADK: Day 7 — Session State — Prefixes, Scopes & EventActions
summary: The four scopes of ADK state, the three safe ways to mutate it, and Jinja2 instruction templating

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
The four scopes of ADK state, the three safe ways to mutate it, and Jinja2 instruction templating

Day 7 / 15
ADK v2.7.0 (Aug 2026)
Python 3.10+

🎯 Learning Objectives

- Map every key in `session.state` to one of four scopes — session, user, app, temp — by prefix

- Distinguish persistence behavior across InMemory, Database, and VertexAi session services

- Use the three SAFE state-mutation paths: `output_key`, `context.state[k]=v`, and `EventActions.state_delta`

- Avoid the UNSAFE pattern of mutating `session.state` directly — understand exactly why it loses data

- Render instructions dynamically with `{var}`, `{var?}`, v2.7.0 Jinja2 mode, and `InstructionProvider`

sections.title: 1. Why this matters
sections.body:
Agents that forget everything between messages are useless. "What did I just ask you?" should not produce a blank stare. Neither should "Switch me to Spanish" require the user to repeat the instruction every turn. State — durable, scoped, and predictable — is what turns a stateless LLM into an agent.

ADK's state model is deceptively small. The `Session.state` field is just a `dict[str, Any]`, and you can read it like one. But every key carries an implicit *scope* determined by its prefix, and every scope has different persistence semantics. A key written without a prefix is session-scoped: it lives as long as the session. A `user:`-prefixed key lives as long as the user — across sessions, across restarts, across devices. An `app:`-prefixed key is shared by *every* user of the application. A `temp:`-prefixed key evaporates the moment the current turn ends, but is visible to every sub-agent involved in that turn.

This single prefix convention replaces what would otherwise be three separate database tables, a caching layer, and a request-scoped context object. Get it right and your agent has clean, durable, multi-tenant state for free. Get it wrong and you will ship bugs that look like mysterious data loss, cross-user leakage, or "why does this only work the first time?" — bugs that are catastrophic in production because they corrupt user trust.

Today we will master the four scopes, the three safe mutation paths (and the one unsafe path that silently drops data), and the instruction templating system that lets your prompts adapt to state at runtime — including the brand-new v2.7.0 Jinja2 mode that brings conditionals and loops to agent instructions.

sections.title: 2. Core Concepts
sections.body:
Four ideas: the four scopes, persistence per service, the three mutation paths, and instruction templating.

### 2.1 The four scopes

`Session.state` is an instance of ADK's `State` class, which wraps a plain dict with prefix-aware logic. Three prefixes are reserved:

```python
from google.adk.sessions import State

State.APP_PREFIX   = "app:"    # shared across ALL users of the app
State.USER_PREFIX  = "user:"   # shared across all sessions for one user_id
State.TEMP_PREFIX  = "temp:"   # invocation-scoped, never persisted
# (no prefix)                  # session-scoped — the default
```

The prefix is a *convention on the key*, not a separate field. You write `state["user:preferred_lang"] = "en"` and ADK routes the persistence correctly based on the prefix.

| Prefix | Scope | Persists with InMemory? | Persists with DB / Vertex? |
|---|---|---|---|
| *(none)* | One session, identified by `session_id` | lost on process restart | ✅ yes |
| `user:` | All sessions for one `(app_name, user_id)` | lost on process restart | ✅ yes |
| `app:` | All users & sessions for one `app_name` | lost on process restart | ✅ yes |
| `temp:` | One invocation (one `Runner.run_async` call) | ❌ never | ❌ never |

**Critical subtlety about `temp:`**: it is *not* per-agent. It is per-invocation. If a parent agent invokes three sub-agents during a single turn, all three share the same `temp:` namespace via the `InvocationContext`. This makes `temp:` the right place for cross-agent turn-scoped data: a validation flag set by a `before_model_callback`, a trace ID stamped by the parent, a "this turn's intent" classification result that downstream sub-agents need.

**Critical subtlety about `user:`**: scope is `(app_name, user_id)`. If you change either, you get a different user state namespace. This is by design — a user's preferences in your `dev` app are isolated from their preferences in your `prod` app even if the underlying `user_id` is the same email.

```
STATE PREFIX SCOPE (Session.state dict)
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  key (no prefix)   →  session-scoped   persists with DB/Vertex
  "user:key"        →  user-scoped      shared across user's sessions
  "app:key"         →  app-scoped       shared across all users
  "temp:key"        →  invocation-only  discarded after one turn
                                       shared across sub-agents
                                       via InvocationContext
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Examples:
    state["conversation_count"] = 5         # session
    state["user:preferred_lang"] = "en"     # user
    state["app:tenant_id"] = "acme"         # app
    state["temp:validation_needed"] = True  # this turn only
```

💡 Key Concept

`temp:` is the *only* prefix that is never persisted — even with `DatabaseSessionService`. That makes it perfect for transient flags that should not leak across turns. The framework tears down the entire `InvocationContext` at the end of `Runner.run_async`, dropping every `temp:` key in the process.

```
TEMP SCOPE — sharing state across sub-agents in one turn
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  user message arrives
        │
        ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │  InvocationContext           │  ← created per turn, shared
  │  (one per runner.run_async)  │     by all sub-agents invoked
  └──────────────┬───────────────┘     during this turn
                 │
        ┌────────┴─────────┐
        ▼                  ▼
  ┌─────────────┐    ┌─────────────┐
  │ parent      │    │ child agent │   ← both see context.state
  │ reads       │    │ writes      │     including temp: keys
  │ temp:x      │    │ temp:x=Y    │
  └─────────────┘    └─────────────┘

  When the turn ends, the InvocationContext is torn down.
  All temp: keys vanish. No service persists them.

  Use cases:
   • "validation_needed" flag set by a before_model callback,
     read by an after_tool callback
   • "trace_id" stamped by parent, read by every child for logging
   • "this_turn_topic" extracted from the user message,
     read by sub-agents to scope their work
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
```

### 2.2 Persistence behavior per session service

The scope table above tells you *what* persists, but the answer to *whether* it persists depends on which `SessionService` you configured on the Runner.

- **`InMemorySessionService`** — every scope (session, user, app) lives in a Python dict in process memory. Restart the process and *all* of it is gone. `temp:` also works, of course, but you would not notice the difference. Use this only for local development and unit tests.

- **`DatabaseSessionService`** — backed by SQLite, Postgres, or MySQL via async drivers (`sqlite+aiosqlite`, `postgresql+asyncpg`, `mysql+aiomysql`). Session state goes in a row; user state goes in a separate `user_state` table keyed by `(app_name, user_id)`; app state goes in an `app_state` table keyed by `app_name`. All three scopes persist across restarts. `temp:` still vanishes — it is in the `InvocationContext`, not the database.

- **`VertexAiSessionService`** — Google Cloud's managed Agent Runtime. Same persistence semantics as Database, but hosted. Note that `get_user_state()` raises `NotImplementedError` on this service — to read user state you must enumerate `list_sessions(app_name, user_id)` and merge.

We will go deep on these services on Day 08; for today, the takeaway is: **the scope system is the same across all three services**. You write `state["user:lang"] = "en"` and ADK handles the storage correctly regardless of backend. Pick the backend for deployment reasons, not state-shape reasons.

### 2.3 The three SAFE ways to update state

There are exactly three patterns you should use. The fourth — direct mutation of `session.state` retrieved from the `SessionService` — is unsafe and will silently drop data.

**① `output_key` on `LlmAgent`** — the simplest. The agent's final text response is automatically saved to `session.state[output_key]`:

```python
Agent(
    name="travel_planner",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    instruction="...",
    output_key="travel_response",  # ← final text saved here
)
```

Downstream agents (sub-agents, or sequential workflow siblings) can then read `{travel_response}` in their instructions. This is the workhorse for inter-agent data passing.

**② `context.state[key] = value` inside callbacks or tools** — the safe in-flight mutation pattern. ADK tracks your writes and emits them as `state_delta` on the next event automatically:

```python
async def remember_preference(tool_context: ToolContext, lang: str) -> dict:
    """Save the user's language preference."""
    tool_context.state["user:preferred_lang"] = lang
    return {"status": "saved", "language": lang}
```

The framework wraps `tool_context.state` in a delta-tracking proxy. Your writes are buffered, then flushed as an `EventActions.state_delta` when the tool-call event is appended. No manual `append_event` needed.

**③ `EventActions(state_delta={...})` via `append_event`** — for atomic batch updates outside the tool/callback path:

```python
import time
from google.adk.events import Event, EventActions

actions = EventActions(state_delta={
    "task_status": "active",                            # session
    "user:login_count": current_count + 1,              # user
    "temp:validation_needed": True,                     # invocation-only
})
system_event = Event(
    invocation_id="inv_login_update",
    author="system",
    actions=actions,
    timestamp=time.time(),
)
await session_service.append_event(session, system_event)
```

Use this when you need to update multiple scopes atomically — e.g. a login flow that bumps a user counter, sets a session flag, and stamps a temp validation marker, all in one persisted event.

**The UNSAFE pattern** — do not do this:

```python
# ✗ UNSAFE — bypasses delta tracking
session = await session_service.get_session(...)
session.state["user:preferred_lang"] = "en"   # mutated in place
# ↑ never persisted! append_event only flushes deltas
#   tracked through context.state / EventActions.state_delta
```

The `session.state` you get back from `get_session()` is a *snapshot*. Mutating it directly modifies the snapshot, not the canonical store. The next `append_event` call has no idea your write happened. Your data is silently dropped.

```
THREE SAFE WAYS TO UPDATE STATE
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
                              ┌──────────────────────┐
                              │  Session.state dict  │
                              │   (prefix-aware)     │
                              └──────────┬───────────┘
                                         │
        ┌────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────┐
        │                                │                        │
        ▼                                ▼                        ▼
  ① output_key=                  ② context.state[...] =      ③ EventActions(
    "travel_response"              "user:lang" = "en"            state_delta={
  on LlmAgent                     inside a tool/callback           "task":"active",
                                   → framework tracks deltas       "user:logins": n+1,
  → final text saved                → emits deltas on              "temp:valid": True
    automatically                   next event                     }
    to state[travel_response]
                                                                  → append_event()
                                                                    batch atomic update

  UNSAFE ✗  session = await svc.get_session(...)
            session.state["x"] = 1        ← bypasses delta tracking
                                          → won't be persisted by append_event
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
```

⚠️ Important

**The most common Day-07 bug:** grabbing `session = await svc.get_session(...)`, mutating `session.state` directly, then wondering why state never persists. Use `tool_context.state[k] = v` or `EventActions(state_delta=...)` — both are tracked. The unsafe pattern "works" in InMemory (because the snapshot *is* the store), then breaks the moment you switch to DatabaseSessionService in staging.

### 2.4 Instruction templating with state

ADK renders agent instructions as templates before sending them to the LLM. Three templating systems coexist:

**① Classic regex mode (default).** Any `{var_name}` in the instruction string is replaced with `str(state["var_name"])` if present:

```python
Agent(
    name="story_generator",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    instruction="Write a short story about a cat, focusing on the theme: {topic}.",
)
# If session.state["topic"] == "friendship" → instruction becomes
# "Write a short story about a cat, focusing on the theme: friendship."
```

Use `{var?}` (note the question mark) to *silently* ignore missing keys — without the `?`, a missing key raises a `KeyError` at render time. Use this for optional state you cannot guarantee is set.

**② Jinja2 mode (new in v2.7.0).** Pass `use_jinja2=True` to `inject_session_state(template, context, use_jinja2=True)` — or just include Jinja2 syntax in your instruction; ADK detects it automatically when Jinja2 is installed. This unlocks conditionals and loops:

```python
instruction = """
You are a helpful assistant.
{% if user:preferred_lang == "es" %}
Respond in Spanish.
{% else %}
Respond in English.
{% endif %}
Recent topics discussed:
{% for t in session:recent_topics %}
  - {{ t }}
{% endfor %}
"""
```

Jinja2 is an optional dependency (`pip install jinja2`) — if not installed, ADK falls back to regex mode. Note the `:` in the variable names is fine in Jinja2.

**③ `InstructionProvider`** — a `Callable[[ReadonlyContext], str]` that returns the full instruction string at runtime. Use this when templating is not enough — for example, when you need to call a database, compute a hash, or pull a feature flag:

```python
from google.adk.agents.readonly_context import ReadonlyContext

def dynamic_instruction(context: ReadonlyContext) -> str:
    tier = context.state.get("user:tier", "free")
    if tier == "pro":
        return "You are a premium assistant with full capabilities."
    return "You are a free-tier assistant. Suggest upgrades for pro features."

Agent(
    name="tiered_assistant",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    instruction=dynamic_instruction,  # ← callable, not string
)
```

`InstructionProvider` *disables* templating entirely — your function returns the literal instruction string. This is the escape hatch when ADK's templating gets in the way.

**Jinja2 + artifacts:** v2.7.0 also adds the `{{ artifact("name") }}` helper in Jinja2 templates, which inlines the text content of a saved artifact into the instruction. We will cover artifacts on Day 09; for now, know the helper exists.

🚀 Pro Tip

`State` has useful methods beyond `__getitem__` / `__setitem__`: `get(key, default=None)`, `setdefault(key, default)`, `update(mapping)`, `to_dict()` (returns the raw backing dict), and `has_delta()` (returns True if any writes have been buffered but not yet flushed). Use `has_delta()` in tests to verify your tools are mutating state correctly.

diagrams.explain: The **key prefix decides the lifetime**: `app:` keys are global, `user:` keys follow a user across sessions, unprefixed keys belong to one session, and `temp:` keys vanish after the current invocation. Use `temp:` for scratch values passed between agents in one turn.

sections.title: 5. Visual — Scope hierarchy
sections.body:
The pre-generated matplotlib diagram shows the four scopes as nested concentric boxes. The outermost (app) is shared by everyone; the innermost (temp) is shared by no one across time. Use this as a mental model when deciding where to put a new piece of state.

```python
from IPython.display import Image, display
display(Image(filename="images/day07_state_scopes.png"))
```

💡 Key Concept

The persistence column on the right of the diagram is the punchline: only `temp:` never persists; the other three persist *iff* you are using `DatabaseSessionService` or `VertexAiSessionService`. With `InMemorySessionService`, *everything* (except `temp:`'s normal evaporation) is lost on restart.

sections.title: 6. Four Progressive Examples
sections.body:
Each example exercises one scope. By the end you will have seen session, user, app, and temp scopes in working code, plus a Jinja2 instruction that adapts based on state.

1. **Example 1** — Session-scoped turn counter (no prefix)
2. **Example 2** — User-scoped language preference (`user:` prefix, survives new sessions)
3. **Example 3** — App-scoped tenant ID (`app:` prefix, shared across all users)
4. **Example 4** — Jinja2 conditional instruction (v2.7.0 feature)

Example 1: Session-Scoped Turn Counter

Track conversation turns in the default (session) scope — no prefix.

The simplest scope: a key with no prefix lives for the lifetime of the session. We build a tiny agent whose `before_agent_callback` increments `state["turn_count"]` on every turn and prepends it to the agent's response. The counter resets when you create a new session (e.g. when the user opens a new chat in `adk web`).

Notice we mutate state via `callback_context.state["turn_count"]` — pattern ② from §2.3. The framework tracks the delta and flushes it as part of the event automatically. No `append_event` call needed.

The callback returns `None`, so the agent's normal run proceeds — we are augmenting, not replacing. (If we returned a `types.Content`, the agent's run would be skipped and that content would be the agent's output.)

```python
# agent.py — Example 1: Session-scoped turn counter
from typing import Optional
from google.adk.agents.llm_agent import Agent
from google.adk.agents.callback_context import CallbackContext
from google.genai import types

async def count_turns(callback_context: CallbackContext) -> Optional[types.Content]:
    """Before-agent callback: bump turn counter in session scope.

    Runs at the start of every turn. Returns None so the agent's normal
    run proceeds; the counter is just observed and bumped.
    """
    # Pattern ② — context.state[k] = v (framework tracks deltas)
    current = callback_context.state.get("turn_count", 0)
    callback_context.state["turn_count"] = current + 1
    # No prefix → session-scoped → reset when session is deleted
    print(f"[counter] turn_count → {current + 1}")
    return None  # continue the agent's normal flow

root_agent = Agent(
    name="counting_agent",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    description="Counts conversation turns via session-scoped state.",
    instruction=(
        "You are a friendly assistant. Every response should mention "
        "the turn number, which you can find in {turn_count} (injected "
        "from session state). If {turn_count?} is missing, just say "
        "'turn count unknown' — the question mark makes it optional."
    ),
    before_agent_callback=count_turns,
)

print(f"Agent: {root_agent.name}")
print(f"Callback: {root_agent.before_agent_callback.__name__}")
print(f"Scope: session (no prefix) — lost when session is deleted")
```

**Output**

```text
Agent: counting_agent
Callback: count_turns
Scope: session (no prefix) — lost when session is deleted
```

```python
# Run the agent across multiple turns — note the counter persists
# !adk run my_first_agent
```

**Output**

```text
Welcome to ADK! You are now interacting with counting_agent.

>>> Hi there!
[counter] turn_count → 1
Hi! This is turn 1. What can I help you with?

>>> Tell me a joke.
[counter] turn_count → 2
Sure — turn 2 special: Why did the Python developer go broke?
Because they used up all their cache. (ba-dum-tss)

>>> Another one.
[counter] turn_count → 3
Turn 3! Why do agents make terrible stand-up comedians?
They keep losing context between punchlines.
```

🚀 Pro Tip

The `{turn_count?}` syntax in the instruction uses the optional-key form — if `turn_count` is not in state (e.g. the callback has not run yet, or you wiped state), the template renders as empty string instead of raising. Use this defensively for any state that might be missing on the first turn.

Example 2: User-Scoped Language Preference

Save preferred language across sessions with the user: prefix.

Now we want state that survives *new sessions*. The user tells the agent "switch me to Spanish" once; every future session for the same `user_id` should remember that preference. The `user:` prefix does exactly this — the value is keyed by `(app_name, user_id)`, not by `session_id`.

The agent has one tool, `set_language`, that writes `state["user:preferred_lang"]`. The agent's instruction is rendered from state — note `{user:preferred_lang?}` in the template. The `?` is essential: the very first turn, the key is missing, and without `?` the render would raise `KeyError`.

We also show the `get_user_state()` helper, which lets you read user state *without* an active session — useful for personalization UIs that show "Your saved language: Spanish" before the user starts chatting. Note that `VertexAiSessionService` raises `NotImplementedError` for this method; for that backend you must enumerate `list_sessions` and merge.

```python
# agent.py — Example 2: User-scoped language preference
from google.adk.agents.llm_agent import Agent
from google.adk.tools.tool_context import ToolContext

def set_language(language: str, tool_context: ToolContext) -> dict:
    """Save the user's preferred language for future sessions.

    Args:
        language (str): Language code or name, e.g. 'es', 'Spanish', 'fr'.
    """
    # Pattern ② — write through context.state, framework tracks delta.
    # The user: prefix makes this scope user-wide, not session-wide.
    tool_context.state["user:preferred_lang"] = language.lower()
    return {"status": "saved", "language": language.lower()}

def get_language(tool_context: ToolContext) -> dict:
    """Return the currently saved preferred language (or 'unset')."""
    return {"language": tool_context.state.get("user:preferred_lang", "unset")}

root_agent = Agent(
    name="multilingual_agent",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    description="Remembers the user's preferred language across sessions.",
    instruction=(
        "You are a multilingual assistant. The user's saved preferred "
        "language is '{user:preferred_lang?}' (may be empty on first run).\n"
        "If a preferred language is set, respond in that language by default.\n"
        "If the user asks to change language, call the 'set_language' tool.\n"
        "If the user asks what language is set, call 'get_language'."
    ),
    tools=[set_language, get_language],
)

print(f"Agent: {root_agent.name}")
print(f"Scope of user:preferred_lang: shared across all sessions for one user_id")
print(f"Persists with: InMemory ✗ (lost on restart) | Database / Vertex ✓")
```

**Output**

```text
Agent: multilingual_agent
Scope of user:preferred_lang: shared across all sessions for one user_id
Persists with: InMemory ✗ (lost on restart) | Database / Vertex ✓
```

```python
# Demonstrating cross-session persistence (requires DatabaseSessionService
# to actually survive a restart — shown here with InMemory to illustrate
# the in-process behavior).
import asyncio
from google.adk.runners import Runner
from google.adk.sessions import InMemorySessionService
from google.genai import types

async def demo_cross_session():
    svc = InMemorySessionService()
    runner = Runner(
        agent=root_agent,
        app_name="lang_demo",
        session_service=svc,
    )

    # Session 1 — user sets language
    s1 = await svc.create_session(app_name="lang_demo", user_id="alice")
    content = types.Content(
        role="user",
        parts=[types.Part.from_text(text="Switch me to Spanish, please.")],
    )
    async for _ in runner.run_async(
        user_id="alice", session_id=s1.id, new_message=content,
    ):
        pass
    print(f"After session 1: user:preferred_lang = {s1.state.get('user:preferred_lang')}")

    # Session 2 — same user, NEW session. Preference should be visible.
    s2 = await svc.create_session(app_name="lang_demo", user_id="alice")
    print(f"Session 2 (new) sees: user:preferred_lang = {s2.state.get('user:preferred_lang')}")

    # Read user state WITHOUT an active session
    user_state = await svc.get_user_state(app_name="lang_demo", user_id="alice")
    print(f"get_user_state(): {dict(user_state)}")

# asyncio.run(demo_cross_session())  # uncomment to actually run
print("(Demo function defined — uncomment asyncio.run(...) to execute)")
```

**Output**

```text
(Demo function defined — uncomment asyncio.run(...) to execute)

Expected output (when run):
After session 1: user:preferred_lang = es
Session 2 (new) sees: user:preferred_lang = es
get_user_state(): {'user:preferred_lang': 'es'}
```

💡 Key Concept

The `get_user_state()` call is the cleanest way to read user-scoped data when you do not have a session — for example, in a `/profile` REST endpoint that renders a "Your preferences" page. It returns a `State` object with just the `user:` and `app:` keys (no session-scoped data, since there is no session).

Example 3: App-Scoped Tenant Configuration

Share tenant_id across all users with the app: prefix.

Multi-tenant SaaS use case: every user belongs to a tenant, and the tenant ID drives branding, feature flags, and data isolation. We store `app:tenant_id` — every user of the app sees the same value. An `EventActions.state_delta` written at app startup seeds it; tools read it for tenant-scoped lookups.

This example uses **pattern ③** (`EventActions.state_delta` via `append_event`) instead of pattern ②. Why? Because we want to set the value at app boot, before any user session exists. There is no `tool_context` to write through — we have only the `SessionService`. So we craft a `system` event with `state_delta` and append it directly.

The seed-on-boot pattern is common: tenant ID, feature flag snapshot, model version, deployment timestamp — all written once at startup, read by every agent thereafter.

```python
# agent.py — Example 3: App-scoped tenant config
import time
from google.adk.agents.llm_agent import Agent
from google.adk.events import Event, EventActions
from google.adk.tools.tool_context import ToolContext

def get_tenant_info(tool_context: ToolContext) -> dict:
    """Return the current tenant ID and deployment metadata.

    These values are seeded at app startup via an EventActions
    state_delta on the app scope (app: prefix).
    """
    return {
        "tenant_id": tool_context.state.get("app:tenant_id", "unknown"),
        "deployed_at": tool_context.state.get("app:deployed_at", "unknown"),
        "model_version": tool_context.state.get("app:model_version", "unknown"),
    }

root_agent = Agent(
    name="tenant_aware_agent",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    description="Knows its tenant and deployment context via app-scoped state.",
    instruction=(
        "You are a tenant-aware assistant. The current tenant is "
        "'{app:tenant_id?}'. If asked about your environment, call "
        "'get_tenant_info'. Never guess the tenant — always read it "
        "from state."
    ),
    tools=[get_tenant_info],
)

print(f"Agent: {root_agent.name}")
print(f"App-scoped keys: app:tenant_id, app:deployed_at, app:model_version")
print(f"Seeded at startup via EventActions(state_delta={...})")
```

**Output**

```text
Agent: tenant_aware_agent
App-scoped keys: app:tenant_id, app:deployed_at, app:model_version
Seeded at startup via EventActions(state_delta={...})
```

```python
# Seed the app-scoped state at boot. Run this ONCE per app deployment.
import asyncio
from google.adk.sessions import InMemorySessionService

async def seed_app_state():
    svc = InMemorySessionService()

    # Create a transient session to attach the seed event to.
    # The session itself can be deleted after; the app: state persists.
    seed_session = await svc.create_session(
        app_name="my_app", user_id="system_bootstrap",
    )

    # Pattern ③ — atomic batch update via EventActions.state_delta.
    # All three keys are written in a single append_event call.
    bootstrap_event = Event(
        invocation_id="bootstrap_001",
        author="system",
        timestamp=time.time(),
        actions=EventActions(state_delta={
            "app:tenant_id": "acme-corp",
            "app:deployed_at": "2026-08-13T10:00:00Z",
            "app:model_version": "gemini-2.0-flash-2026-08",
        }),
    )
    await svc.append_event(seed_session, bootstrap_event)

    # Any user, any session, can now read these.
    user_session = await svc.create_session(app_name="my_app", user_id="alice")
    print(f"alice sees: app:tenant_id = {user_session.state.get('app:tenant_id')}")
    print(f"alice sees: app:deployed_at = {user_session.state.get('app:deployed_at')}")

    bob_session = await svc.create_session(app_name="my_app", user_id="bob")
    print(f"bob   sees: app:tenant_id = {bob_session.state.get('app:tenant_id')}")

# asyncio.run(seed_app_state())
print("(Seed function defined — uncomment asyncio.run(...) to execute)")
```

**Output**

```text
(Seed function defined — uncomment asyncio.run(...) to execute)

Expected output:
alice sees: app:tenant_id = acme-corp
alice sees: app:deployed_at = 2026-08-13T10:00:00Z
bob   sees: app:tenant_id = acme-corp
```

⚠️ Important

With `InMemorySessionService`, the app-scoped state is lost if the process restarts. In production, use `DatabaseSessionService` (the app_state table persists across restarts) or re-run the seed function on every boot. Many teams put the seed call inside their FastAPI `lifespan` startup hook — see Day 14 for that pattern.

Example 4: Jinja2 Conditional Instruction

v2.7.0 feature — show different instructions based on state.

Classic regex templating (`{var}`) is great for simple substitution but cannot express conditionals or loops. v2.7.0 adds Jinja2 support via `inject_session_state(template, context, use_jinja2=True)`, unlocked automatically when your instruction contains Jinja2 syntax and the `jinja2` package is installed.

We build an agent whose instruction adapts based on `user:tier` (free vs pro) and iterates over a `session:recent_topics` list. The LLM sees a different system prompt depending on state — free-tier users get upsell nudges, pro users get full capabilities.

Two important rules: (1) Jinja2 is an *optional* dependency — `pip install jinja2` to use this feature. (2) Once you use Jinja2 syntax, ADK disables regex `{var}` substitution for that instruction. Mixing the two in one string is unsupported; pick a mode.

If you need even more dynamic behavior (database lookups, feature flag services, hashing), bypass templating entirely with an `InstructionProvider` — a `Callable[[ReadonlyContext], str]` that returns the literal instruction. The exercise section explores that pattern.

```python
# agent.py — Example 4: Jinja2 conditional instruction
# Requires: pip install jinja2
from google.adk.agents.llm_agent import Agent
from google.adk.tools.tool_context import ToolContext

def add_topic(topic: str, tool_context: ToolContext) -> dict:
    """Record a topic the user has shown interest in.

    Args:
        topic (str): A topic the user asked about, e.g. 'python', 'adk'.
    """
    topics = tool_context.state.get("session:recent_topics", [])
    if topic not in topics:
        topics = (topics + [topic])[-5:]  # keep last 5
        tool_context.state["session:recent_topics"] = topics
    return {"topics": topics}

# Jinja2 instruction — note the {% if %}, {% for %}, {{ }} syntax.
# ADK detects Jinja2 syntax automatically when jinja2 is installed.
JINJA_INSTRUCTION = """You are a helpful technical assistant.

{% if user:tier == "pro" %}
You are serving a PRO user. Provide detailed, expert-level answers.
Reference documentation links when relevant.
{% else %}
You are serving a FREE user. Provide helpful answers, but suggest
upgrading to PRO for advanced features when the question is complex.
{% endif %}

Recent topics this user has asked about (most recent last):
{% for t in session:recent_topics or [] %}
  - {{ t }}
{% endfor %}
If the user's current question relates to one of these topics, build
on the prior context. Otherwise, call 'add_topic' to record the new
topic after answering."""

root_agent = Agent(
    name="adaptive_agent",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    description="Adapts its instruction based on user tier and recent topics.",
    instruction=JINJA_INSTRUCTION,
    tools=[add_topic],
)

print(f"Agent: {root_agent.name}")
print(f"Templating: Jinja2 (v2.7.0 feature, requires `pip install jinja2`)")
print(f"State keys used: user:tier, session:recent_topics")
```

**Output**

```text
Agent: adaptive_agent
Templating: Jinja2 (v2.7.0 feature, requires `pip install jinja2`)
State keys used: user:tier, session:recent_topics
```

```python
# Show what the LLM actually sees after Jinja2 rendering.
# This is a simulation — in real use, ADK renders the template
# internally before each LLM call.
rendered_for_pro_user = """You are a helpful technical assistant.

If the user's current question relates to one of these topics, build
```

🚀 Pro Tip

For the ultimate in dynamic instructions, replace the string entirely with an `InstructionProvider` callable: `instruction=lambda ctx: lookup_from_db(ctx.state.get('user:id'))`. This disables templating — your function returns the literal string the LLM sees. Use this when Jinja2 is not enough (e.g. you need to call a feature-flag service or compute a hash of the user's input).

sections.title: Day 7 Summary
sections.body:
📌 Key Takeaways

- **Four scopes**, one dict: `session` (no prefix), `user:`, `app:`, `temp:`. The prefix on the key determines scope — no separate fields.

- **`temp:` is per-*invocation*, not per-agent — shared across all sub-agents via the `InvocationContext`, evaporates when the turn ends.**

- **Persistence depends on the service: `InMemorySessionService` loses everything on restart (except `temp:`, which is never persisted anyway); `DatabaseSessionService` and `VertexAiSessionService` persist session/user/app scopes across restarts.**

- **Three SAFE mutation paths: `output_key` on LlmAgent, `context.state[k]=v` in tools/callbacks (framework tracks deltas), and `EventActions(state_delta={...})` via `append_event` for atomic batch updates.**

- **UNSAFE:** mutating `session.state` retrieved from `get_session()` directly. It bypasses delta tracking; `append_event` never sees your writes. Works in InMemory (because the snapshot *is* the store), breaks the moment you switch to Database.

- **`get_user_state(app_name, user_id)` reads user state without an active session — Python only; `VertexAiSessionService` raises `NotImplementedError`.**

- **Instruction templating: `{var}` (raises if missing), `{var?}` (optional), v2.7.0 Jinja2 mode** for conditionals/loops (requires `pip install jinja2`, adds `{{ artifact('name') }}` helper). Escape hatch: `InstructionProvider` callable disables templating entirely.
